chunks: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Abū Jamīlah, from Abū Usāmah, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning:

A man who killed a believer intentionally while knowing that he was a believer, except that anger drove him to kill him—does he have any tawbah, and what is his tawbah if he wishes to repent, or does he have no tawbah?

He said: “Retaliation is carried out against him. If it was not known about him, he should go to his heirs and inform them that he killed him. If they pardon him, he should give them the blood-money, free a slave, fast two consecutive months, and give charity to sixty needy persons.”

key_terms.الدِّيَةَ: blood-money; financial compensation paid to the heirs if they pardon
key_terms.الْغَضَبُ: anger; the motive that drove the act without removing responsibility
key_terms.تَوْبَةٍ: repentance; the offender’s path of return through legal and expiatory fulfillment
key_terms.سِتِّينَ مِسْكِينًا: sixty needy persons; those to whom charity is given as expiation
key_terms.شَهْرَيْنِ مُتَتَابِعَيْنِ: two consecutive months; the required expiatory fasting
key_terms.مُؤْمِنًا: a believer; the victim whose sanctity is fully recognized
key_terms.يُقَادُ: retaliatory punishment is carried out; referring to qisas

ai.seo_question: What is the tawbah for someone who intentionally kills a believer in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith gives the legal ruling regarding one who intentionally kills a believer while knowing his faith, even if anger was the immediate cause. It establishes that tawbah is not merely inward remorse, but includes submitting to qisas or informing the victim’s heirs, fulfilling financial compensation, and performing expiatory acts.
